extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of ancient Greek philosophy; theorists and practitioners of comedy/humor
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Aristotle's criteria for the geloion (the laughable) to evaluate or produce comic material: identify real faults that are non-painful and non-destructive, maintain proper social distance, and exercise eutrapelia (taste). Also use the Tractatus Coislinianus' verbal and material sources as techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining formula (Poetics 1449a32-37)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comedy is, as we said, an imitation of inferior people — not, however, in the full sense of the word bad, but the laughable is a species of the base or ugly. It consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the core definition: comedy imitates 'inferior' people or states, centered on a defect/ugliness; that defect must not produce pain or destruction. This formula frames all other tests—comic material should aim at a non-harmful, non-ruinous blemish or mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartēma (the mistake/blemish must be real)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be an actual fault, error, ignorance, or unseemliness present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The laughable should be grounded in a recognisable defect or error rather than pure absurdity with no anchor. Avoid jokes that rely on fabricated 'faults' that the audience cannot recognise as a plausible mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anōdunon — not painful
rubrics_metrics.description: The defect or ugliness must be not painful (anōdunon) — neither to the agent nor to the spectator at the moment of perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the audience perceives suffering or pity, the comic framing collapses and tends toward tragedy. Avoid inflicting or foregrounding real suffering when seeking laughter; borderline discomfort risks turning reactions into pity rather than mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ou phthartikon — not destructive
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable must not be destructive — it does not cause ruin, death, or major harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes whose object or situation involves serious ruin, permanent loss, or mortal danger are disqualified from the comic mode. Ensure consequences remain trivial or reversible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belongs to the inferior (hoi phauloi)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic mode imitates people worse than ourselves (the 'inferior'); we look down without strong negative emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a painless distance: targets should be socially or morally inferior enough to permit ridicule without provoking anger or sympathy. Avoid mocking those too close to the audience or those held in high regard—proximity or nobility erodes the comic frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collapse conditions (what destroys the joke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that collapse the comic frame: if the mistake causes visible suffering (slides into pity/tragedy); if it destroys someone or something important; if the target is too noble or close to us (loss of painless distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an anti-pattern checklist. When evaluating material, ask whether any of these factors are present; their presence typically disqualifies the passage as comic and may instead evoke pity, anger, or tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eutrapelia — the well-bred wit (mean between vices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The witty person (eutrapelos) is the mean between buffoon (bōmolochos) and boor (agroikos): jokes only at things appropriate to a free person, never at what a free person would be ashamed of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspire to tasteful wit: avoid the buffoon's indiscriminate joke-making and the boor's joylessness. Evaluate jokes for appropriateness to social role and decorum; tasteful restraint is itself a criterion of good comic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tractatus Coislinianus — verbal sources of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal sources: homonymy, synonymy, garrulity, paronyms (additions/clippings), diminutives, perversion of word, grammar/syntax errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are technical linguistic techniques that can produce laughter. Use wordplay (homonyms, paronyms), diminutives, deliberate grammar slips, or semantic perversions, but ensure they still satisfy the conditions of non-pain and non-destruction and are aimed suitably (eutrapelia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tractatus Coislinianus — material sources of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Material sources: assimilation (worse/better), deception, the impossible, the possible-but-inconsequent, things contrary to expectation, debasing personae, choice of vulgar dancing, when the powerful pass over great matters and choose the worthless, when the story is disjointed and lacks sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These situational devices generate comic effect (incongruity, reversal, bathos, absurd sequence). Apply them to produce non-harmful blemishes/errors; watch that the scenario remains non-destructive and maintains social distance so that laughter, not pity or outrage, results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist (practical questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a real fault, mistake, or ugliness present? Does the audience feel pain or pity at the moment of laughter? Is anyone or anything actually being destroyed? Does the joker show eutrapelia (taste) rather than bōmolochia (will to laugh at anything)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a quick evaluative tool for existing material or during composition. Affirmative answers to the first and negative answers to the others indicate the material fits Aristotle's laughable; failures point to needed revision (soften harm, increase distance, refine target).
